overview.title: A brief history of NLP: from hand-written rules to machine learning
overview.section: 14.1 A brief history of natural language processing
overview.main_topic: Why natural language is messy, what NLP is, and how the field moved from hand-crafted symbolic rules (the 1954 Georgetown-IBM demo, the funding collapse) to data-driven machine learning in the late 1980s.
overview.central_idea: Natural language evolved through use, and its rules were formalised afterward and are often broken, so it is ambiguous and constantly changing. Early NLP tried to write down 'the rule set of English' and failed to generalise beyond handpicked examples. Once computers and data grew, engineers began searching for rules automatically from corpora, which is machine learning.
overview.importance: It gives the historical argument for the rest of the text chapters: hand-written rules cannot capture language, and learning from data can. It also repeats the book's chapter 1 view of machine learning as automatically searching for rules and representations (p.27-p.30).
learning_objectives: Explain why natural language is 'messy' compared with machine languages.
Define NLP and describe its post-WWII 'code-cracking' origins.
Recount the Georgetown-IBM demonstration and why rule-based translation failed to generalise.
Explain why handcrafted rules persisted into the 1990s despite their problems.
Describe the conceptual shift from writing rules to searching for rules in a rule space using a corpus.
prerequisites: The definition of machine learning as learning rules from data (chapter 1, p.27-p.30)
The chapter opener's contrast between designed and natural languages (p.405)

summary:
The page completes the contrast begun on p.405. With human language **usage comes first and rules arise later**. Natural language was shaped by an evolutionary process, like biological organisms, which is what makes it "natural." Its grammar was formalised after the fact and is often ignored or broken. So while machine-readable language is structured and rigorous, natural language is **messy: ambiguous, chaotic, sprawling, and constantly in flux**.

Computer scientists have long wanted systems that can read or produce language, because text underpins most communication and culture, stores centuries of knowledge, and makes up most of the internet. Using computers to interpret and manipulate language is **natural language processing (NLP)**. It was proposed as a field right after World War II, when some saw understanding language as **"code cracking"**.

Early researchers naively thought you could write down **"the rule set of English"** the way one writes down LISP's. In the early 1950s, **IBM and Georgetown** demonstrated Russian-to-English translation using **six hardcoded grammar rules** and a **lookup table of a couple of hundred words and suffixes**, which correctly translated **60 handpicked sentences**. The demo succeeded at raising excitement and funding, and its authors claimed translation would be solved within five years. Funding flowed for nearly a decade, but generalisation proved "maddeningly difficult": word meanings change with context and every grammar rule needs countless exceptions. An influential US report a decade later criticised the lack of progress, and funding dried up.

Even so, **handcrafted rules remained dominant into the 1990s**, simply because there was no viable alternative. In the late 1980s, faster computers and more data opened a new direction. An engineer facing "big piles of ad hoc rules" naturally asks whether a **corpus** could automate finding them, by **searching a rule space** instead of inventing rules by hand. That is machine learning. The first ML approaches to NLP, in the late 1980s, were based on **decision trees**. The sentence continues on p.407.

paragraphs.excerpt: it’s the reverse: usage comes first, and rules arise later. Natural
paragraphs.what_it_says: Continuing from p.405: for human language, usage comes first and rules arise later. Natural language was shaped by an evolutionary process, like biological organisms, which is what makes it 'natural'. Its rules, like English grammar, were formalised after the fact and are often ignored or broken. So machine languages are structured and rigorous, while natural language is messy: ambiguous, chaotic, sprawling and constantly in flux.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Grammar describes how a language has been used. It doesn't define the language. That's why any fixed rule set will always be incomplete and go out of date as the language changes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This messiness is the problem every NLP technique in the coming chapters has to deal with, and the reason learned statistical models replaced hand-written grammars.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): ambiguity shows up at every level. Lexical: 'bank'. Syntactic: 'I saw the man with the telescope'. Pragmatic: sarcasm. A rule system has to resolve each case explicitly, while a statistical model learns from context which reading is most likely.

terminology.meaning: Rules written down to describe existing usage rather than to define the language beforehand.

connections: p.405: the first half of the contrast: machine languages were designed rules-first

paragraphs.excerpt: Computer scientists have long fixated on the potential of systems that
paragraphs.what_it_says: Computer scientists have long been drawn to systems that can take in or produce natural language. Written text underpins most communication and culture, stores centuries of knowledge, makes up most of the internet, and 'even our thoughts are based on language'. Using computers to interpret and manipulate language is NLP. It was proposed as a field right after World War II, when some viewed understanding language as 'code cracking', with natural language as the code that carries information.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The paragraph explains why NLP matters (text is the main way humanity stores and exchanges knowledge) and where its first framing came from: wartime cryptanalysis, which suggested that translation might be just a matter of decoding.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The code-cracking framing explains the early optimism. If language is a code, a fixed set of decoding rules should be enough. The next paragraph shows why that was wrong.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the claim that 'our thoughts are based on language' is a strong philosophical position that is debated in cognitive science. Read it as the authors' rhetorical emphasis rather than settled fact.

terminology.meaning: The practice of using computers to interpret and manipulate human language.
The post-WWII view of language understanding as decryption: natural language as a code for information.

connections: p.407: the modern view of NLP as pattern recognition applied to words

paragraphs.excerpt: In the early days of the field, many people naively thought
paragraphs.what_it_says: Early on, many people thought you could write down 'the rule set of English' like LISP's. In the early 1950s, IBM and Georgetown researchers demonstrated Russian-to-English translation with six hardcoded grammar rules and a lookup table of a couple of hundred words and suffixes, correctly translating 60 handpicked sentences. The demo raised excitement and funding, and its authors claimed translation would be solved within five years. Funding poured in for most of a decade, but generalising proved maddeningly difficult: meanings depend on context and grammar rules need countless exceptions. Doing well on handpicked examples was easy, but a robust system competitive with human translators was not. An influential US report a decade later criticised the lack of progress, and funding dried up.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is an early example of overfitting at the level of a whole research programme. A system tuned to 60 curated sentences told you almost nothing about performance on real text. The gap between demo and deployment is the gap between training-set and test-set performance.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It's a cautionary tale about hype and evaluation that echoes the book's warnings elsewhere about short-term hype (p.36) and about judging models on data they haven't seen.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the demonstration took place in 1954, and the 'influential US report' is generally identified as the 1966 ALPAC report. The book itself gives no names or exact dates.

terminology.meaning: A fixed mapping from source words or suffixes to target equivalents.
Examples chosen in advance to work well, the opposite of an unbiased test set.

connections: p.27: chapter 1 notes symbolic AI struggled with fuzzy problems like natural language translation
p.36: chapter 1's warning about short-term hype

paragraphs.excerpt: Despite these setbacks and repeated swings from excitement to disillusionment, handcrafted
paragraphs.what_it_says: Despite setbacks and repeated cycles of excitement and disillusionment, handcrafted rules stayed dominant into the 1990s. The problems were obvious, but there was no viable alternative to writing symbolic grammar rules. In the late 1980s, faster computers and more data pushed research in a new direction. An engineer building 'big piles of ad hoc rules' will start asking whether a corpus could automate finding these rules, by searching a rule space instead of inventing rules. That is machine learning.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Machine learning arose here as an engineering response to rule maintenance becoming unmanageable. Instead of a human writing rules, an algorithm searches a space of candidate rules and keeps those that agree with the data. It's the same definition of ML the book gives in chapter 1.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It connects NLP's history to the book's core idea of learning representations and rules from data, and explains why progress depended on compute and data becoming available.
paragraphs.technical_idea: 'Search for the rules within some rule space' corresponds to the book's notion of a hypothesis space. Learning is a search through it, guided by feedback from data (p.30).

terminology.meaning: A large collection of text used as data.
The set of candidate rules a learning algorithm can choose from, i.e. a hypothesis space.
Explicit, human-written if/then rules over symbols such as words and grammatical categories.

connections: p.30: chapter 1 defines machine learning as searching for useful representations and rules, guided by feedback
p.27: symbolic AI dominated until the late 1980s

paragraphs.excerpt: In the late 1980s, we started seeing machine learning approaches to
paragraphs.what_it_says: The first machine learning approaches to NLP appeared in the late 1980s. The earliest were based on decision trees, whose intent was literally to (continued on p.407) automate the development of the if/then/else rules of hardcoded systems.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Decision trees were a natural bridge: they produce the same kind of if/then/else logic as hand-written systems, but learned from data. The next step (p.407) is statistical models such as logistic regression.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows the field moving gradually from rules to learned parameters, which leads to the neural models of this chapter.

terminology.meaning: A model that predicts by following a learned sequence of if/then/else tests on input features.

connections: p.407: continuation — statistical approaches, logistic regression, and learned parametric models taking over

concepts.name: Natural language processing (NLP)
concepts.definition: The practice of using computers to interpret and manipulate language.
concepts.intuition: Getting computers to work with language as people really use it.
concepts.technical: Began after WWII under a 'code cracking' framing. Rule-based until the late 1980s, then increasingly learned from data.
concepts.significance: Text holds most human knowledge and communication.
concepts.example: Russian-to-English machine translation, the field's early flagship goal.
concepts.misconception: That language is a code that a fixed rule set can decode.

concepts.name: Rule-based (symbolic) NLP
concepts.definition: NLP systems built from hand-written grammar rules and lookup tables.
concepts.intuition: Writing a complete instruction manual for a language.
concepts.technical: The Georgetown-IBM demo used 6 rules and a few hundred lexicon entries for 60 sentences. Such systems didn't generalise because meanings depend on context and rules need endless exceptions.
concepts.significance: Dominant into the 1990s for lack of alternatives. Its failure motivated ML.
concepts.example: A rule 'Russian suffix X becomes English ending Y' that breaks on irregular words.
concepts.misconception: That a working demo on curated examples shows the approach works in general.

concepts.name: Machine learning as rule search
concepts.definition: Using a corpus of data to automatically find rules within a rule space, instead of writing them by hand.
concepts.intuition: Instead of writing the rules, show the computer examples and let it figure out the rules.
concepts.technical: Equivalent to searching a hypothesis space guided by feedback from data (p.30).
concepts.significance: The shift that made modern NLP possible once compute and data grew in the late 1980s.
concepts.example: Decision trees learning if/then/else rules for language from annotated text.
concepts.misconception: That ML replaces structure with magic. It's a systematic search over candidate rules.

deeper.title: Timeline of the history on this page
deeper.body:
| When (book's wording) | Event |
|---|---|
| Right after WWII | NLP proposed as a field; language seen as 'code cracking' |
| Early 1950s | IBM-Georgetown Russian→English demo: 6 rules, ~200-entry lookup table, 60 handpicked sentences |
| Following decade | Funding pours in; claims that translation will be solved in five years |
| A decade later | Influential US report criticises lack of progress; funding dries up |
| Into the 1990s | Handcrafted rules remain dominant |
| Late 1980s | Faster computers and more data → first ML approaches (decision trees) |
| Continues on p.407 | Logistic regression, learned parametric models |

Beyond the book: the demo is usually dated to 1954 and the report identified as ALPAC (1966).

deeper.title: The Georgetown demo as a generalisation failure
deeper.body: Picture a student who memorises the answers to the 60 questions they know will be on the test. They score perfectly and impress everyone, then fail completely on new questions. The Georgetown-IBM system was in the same position: tuned to handpicked sentences, it said nothing about performance on real text. In machine learning terms, it was evaluated on its own training data.

visualizations.title: From writing rules to learning them
visualizations.why: Shows the sequence the page describes: hand-written symbolic rules, the generalisation failure, and the shift to searching for rules with data (continued on p.407).

misconceptions.claim: Natural language has a complete set of grammar rules that a program could implement.
misconceptions.correction: Its rules were formalised after the fact, are often broken, and keep changing. Natural language is ambiguous and in flux.

misconceptions.claim: The Georgetown-IBM demo showed that rule-based translation worked.
misconceptions.correction: It worked only on 60 handpicked sentences. Generalising proved maddeningly difficult and funding later dried up.

misconceptions.claim: Rule-based NLP was abandoned as soon as its problems became clear.
misconceptions.correction: It stayed dominant into the 1990s because there was no viable alternative until compute and data grew.

earlier.note: Opening contrast between designed machine languages and natural languages.
Symbolic AI and its failure on fuzzy problems like translation.
Machine learning as searching for rules and representations with feedback.

later.note: Statistical NLP, the Jelinek quote, modern NLP as pattern recognition, LSTMs and Transformers.

prerequisites.note: Learning rules and representations from data (chapter 1).

takeaways: Natural language evolved usage-first. Its rules came later and are often broken, so it is messy.
NLP means using computers to interpret and manipulate language. It began after WWII with a code-cracking view.
The 1950s Georgetown-IBM demo (6 rules, about 200 lexicon entries, 60 handpicked sentences) produced hype that collapsed when generalisation failed.
Handcrafted rules lasted into the 1990s for lack of alternatives.
From the late 1980s, compute and data enabled searching for rules with a corpus, i.e. machine learning, starting with decision trees.

questions.question: What did the early-1950s IBM-Georgetown translation system consist of?
options: A neural network trained on parallel corpora
Six hardcoded grammar rules and a lookup table of a couple of hundred words and suffixes
A decision tree learned from Russian newspapers
A statistical model based on logistic regression
questions.answer: Six hardcoded grammar rules and a lookup table of a couple of hundred words and suffixes
questions.explanation: That's exactly how the page describes it. Neural networks, decision trees and logistic regression came decades later. The page puts decision trees in the late 1980s, and p.407 puts logistic regression after that.

questions.question: Why did rule-based translation systems fail to generalise beyond handpicked examples?
questions.answer: Words change meaning dramatically with context, and any grammar rule needs countless exceptions, so a small rule set that worked on curated sentences couldn't handle real text robustly.
questions.explanation: The page gives these two reasons explicitly.

questions.question: Why did handcrafted rules remain dominant into the 1990s even though their problems were obvious?
questions.answer: There was no viable alternative. Learning rules from data needed faster computers and more data, which only became available in the late 1980s.
questions.explanation: The page says there was 'simply no viable alternative' until compute and data grew.

questions.question: How does the page's description of the shift to machine learning ('search for the rules within some rule space') match the book's general definition of machine learning?
questions.answer: Both describe ML as an automatic search, guided by data, through a space of possible rules or representations, instead of having a human write the rules.
questions.explanation: Chapter 1 (p.30) frames ML as systematically searching for representations and rules using feedback. This page applies that framing to NLP.

questions.question: What makes natural language 'natural', according to the authors?
options: It is spoken rather than written
It was shaped by an evolutionary process, with usage first and rules later
It is processed by the human brain
questions.answer: It was shaped by an evolutionary process, with usage first and rules later
questions.explanation: The page says natural language evolved much like biological organisms, which is what makes it natural. It does have grammar, but formalised after the fact. Being spoken or processed by the brain isn't the authors' criterion.

questions.question: Can you connect the Georgetown-IBM story to the ML idea of evaluating on held-out data?
questions.answer: The demo was judged on 60 handpicked sentences it was designed for, like evaluating on training data. Real performance on unseen text was far worse, which is why held-out test sets matter.
questions.explanation: This is an interpretation (not stated by the authors) linking the history to evaluation practice taught in chapter 5.

questions.question: What were the earliest machine learning approaches to NLP based on, and what was their aim?
questions.answer: Decision trees, aiming to automate the development of the if/then/else rules that hardcoded language systems used.
questions.explanation: Stated at the bottom of this page and continued at the top of p.407.
